topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Bouncing Blocks Count Digits of Pi
target_audience: High school or undergraduate students with basic physics and geometry knowledge

outline.topic: The Pi-Collision Paradox: Why Bouncing Blocks Count Digits of Pi
outline.target_audience: High school or undergraduate students with basic physics and geometry knowledge

sections.title: The Hook: An Impossible Counting Puzzle
sections.content: Introduce the physical system: Two blocks of different masses (M1 and M2) on a frictionless surface. M1 moves toward M2, which is next to a wall. How many collisions occur until they stop moving toward each other?
sections.example: Scenario: A small 'Mouse' block (mass 1) sliding toward a massive 'Elephant' block (mass 100, 10,000, etc.) waiting near a wall.

sections.title: Prerequisite Setup: Momentum and Energy
sections.content: Briefly review elastic collision laws (Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy). Define the visual representation: The 'Phase Space' of the two blocks as a triangle in a 2D coordinate system.
sections.example: Visual: A graph where the x-axis is the velocity of block 1 and the y-axis is the velocity of block 2. Each collision is a 'bounce' against the boundaries of an energy-conserving sector.

sections.title: The Geometric Transformation
sections.content: Explain that as the ratio of mass M2/M1 increases by powers of 100, the path of the blocks traces a zigzag that perfectly fits the arc of a circle. The number of collisions corresponds to the digits of Pi.
sections.example: Animation: If mass ratio is 1:1, we get 3 collisions. If 1:100, we get 31 collisions. If 1:10,000, we get 314 collisions.

sections.title: Connecting Physics to Pi
sections.content: Explain why this happens: The total energy constraint defines a circular boundary in the phase space. The discrete collisions represent the approximation of the arc length or the angle swept, which is directly proportional to Pi.
sections.example: Visual: Overlay a circular protractor onto the 'bouncing' path of the blocks in phase space to show how the segments intersect the circumference.

sections.title: Conclusion and Deep Insight
sections.content: Summarize that Pi is not just a circle property but a universal constant emerging from symmetry and conservation laws, even in seemingly unrelated linear movement problems.
sections.example: Final slide: 'Nature hides Pi in the most unexpected places.' Show a final visualization of a block with mass 10^8 yielding the first 9 digits of Pi (3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5).

storyboard.title: The Hook: An Impossible Counting Puzzle
lecture_lines: Two blocks slide on a frictionless surface.
One block moves toward a wall-bound block.
How many collisions happen before they stop?
animations: Animate two squares appearing on a dark background #000000. Labels: 'm1' in #FF00FF and 'm2' in #00FFFF.
Slide block 'm1' toward block 'm2' at a constant speed.
Add a wall label near 'm2' and show a collision count #FFFFFF.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Setup: Momentum and Energy
lecture_lines: Conservation of momentum governs elastic collisions.
Conservation of kinetic energy limits block motion.
Phase space visuals map these constraints perfectly.
animations: Show equation p = mv in #FFFF00 for momentum.
Show equation K = 1/2mv^2 in #00FF00 for energy.
Display an empty graph grid #808080 representing phase space.

storyboard.title: The Geometric Transformation
lecture_lines: Mass ratios determine the collision count.
The path length traces digits of Pi.
Higher ratios yield more digits of Pi.
animations: Display two mass blocks showing ratio 1:100.
Draw a circular arc inside the phase space grid #FF9900.
Animate a vector tracing the path length calculation.
Highlight the number 31 on the screen in #FF0000.
Show a progression of digits 3.1415... appearing near the path.

storyboard.title: Connecting Physics to Pi
lecture_lines: Energy constraints form a circular boundary.
Collisions represent the arc length approximation.
The geometry reflects Pi's hidden presence.
Phase space angles track the collisions.
Each bounce maps to a Pi digit.
animations: Draw a circle on the grid labeled 'Energy Constraint' #00FFFF.
Flash a light path connecting two collision points.
Superimpose the Pi symbol over the geometric arc #FF00FF.
Highlight phase space coordinates changing after each bounce.
Connect each bounce to a digit 3, 1, 4.

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Deep Insight
lecture_lines: Pi emerges from simple physical symmetry.
Conservation laws dictate these complex patterns.
Nature hides Pi in linear motion.
animations: Show Pi symbol #FF00FF merging with a colliding block.
Highlight conservation formulas disappearing into a geometric arc.
Final wide view showing the full phase space Pi path #FFFFFF.
